(b) baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate (last updated Sept 22, 2025): after excluding the "just browsing" segment, "40% Extra costs too high (shipping, tax, fees)" is the top reason; population is US online shoppers. 'delivery', items)` — identical arithmetic to what the recommendation proposes for the cart, so the cart figure would be exactly the charged figure for the default path. All numbers (₪29, ₪0 pickup, free ≥ ₪550 measured on list price, ₪49 gift box, 5 installments) come from lib/policy.ts, lib/extras.ts and the truth sheet. No review/urgency/scarcity/invented claim is introduced. Effort "small" is right: one file, ~60 lines.

Hard-rule angle that actually strengthens it: the current cart line «עד 5 תשלומים של כ־₪60» is itself a number that is untrue on the default delivery path (5×60=300, charged 328 → ₪65.60/payment); fixing it is compliance, not just CRO.

CLAIMS THAT DO NOT HOLD: (1) "Observed live: per-installment figure changes from ₪60 to ₪66" — false as an observation; CheckoutForm renders no installment line at all (grep: perInstallment only in ProductView and CartDrawer). ₪66 is an inference (round(328/5)), and Grow is not connected yet, so nothing on the site shows it. (2) "the purchase path currently asks eight decisions" — not derivable; I count 11 optional prompts (blessing, finish, qty×2, gift×2, code, shipping method, recipient, terms, marketing) of which 2 are mandatory. (3) Dhar 1997 (JCR 24(2):215-231, verified real: https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/24/2/215/1794929) is mis-paraphrased: the abstract says deferral tracks closeness of alternatives' attractiveness and is "not consistent with trade-off difficulty"; it says nothing about the number of steps in a checkout. (4) Baymard guideline #836 is paywalled; its public blurb concerns free-shipping visibility on PRODUCT pages, not a cart rule "alongside threshold info" — unverifiable. (5) Baymard abandonment figures are correct (40% "Extra costs too high", 12% "couldn't see / calculate total order cost up-front", https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) but are for US online shoppers and the page states no year/sample size — cite without a year. 1. Simonson 1992 (MIT PDF, read in full): figures are exact — 218 undergrads, wedding present for a close relative, July purchase 54% control vs 63% regret condition (Table 1), brand task 50%→67%. HOWEVER the effect was produced by asking subjects which error they would regret more (plus telling them they'd get feedback), in a scenario where 'the store did not accept returns on sale items'. The paper never tests reversibility; the proposed line is the opposite intervention (it removes the regret stake rather than eliciting it). Also a single 1992 study, t=2.0 p<.05, and the logit counted each subject's 4 choices as independent observations (n=235 obs from ~55 students). 54→63 must not be presented as the expected lift of a reversibility line.

2. Givi & Galak 2017: mechanism correctly described (givers uncertain a sentimental gift will land — 'home runs or strikeouts' vs 'a sure single', per sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/07/170725100701.htm). But 'shrinking the downside flips the choice' is not what they did: Study 3 primed a risk-taking mindset (writing about risks that succeeded vs failed). Outcome is WHICH gift is chosen, not whether to buy.

3. Ou, Pavlou & Davison 2014 (aisel.aisnet.org/misq/vol38/iss1/12): Taobao, China, N=338; IM effective use → interactivity/presence → swift guanxi + trust → REPURCHASE intentions and actual repurchases. Not first purchase from an unknown seller, not the mere presence of a chat link, and guanxi is a culture-specific construct. Overstated.

4. Chernev et al. 2015 (PDF read): 99 observations, 53 studies, N=7202, four moderators — exact. But it is a meta-analysis of ASSORTMENT SIZE (large vs small sets); the chooser has 2–5 options and the change does not alter assortment. Preference uncertainty is operationalized as expertise / articulated ideal point — plausibly high for a gift buyer, but 'by definition' is the recommender's inference, not the paper's.

votes.reason:
The action (check the sticky bar on a phone, log it) is sound and cheap, but the recommendation overstates both its evidence and its urgency.

SOURCES CHECKED
1. Vohs et al. 2021 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12422598/) — figures are exact: "k = 36; N = 3,531", "nonsignificant result (d = 0.06)", exploratory full-sample d = 0.08, Bayes factor 4.4 for the null. It supports only the negative half of the claim ("depletion is not reliable"). It says nothing about deferral, task difficulty, or distance.
2. Dhar 1997, JCR 24(2):215 (https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/24/2/215/1794929) — the paraphrase is inverted. The abstract states deferral "is influenced by the absolute difference in attractiveness among the alternatives provided and is NOT consistent with trade-off difficulty or the theory of search." It is original lab work on hypothetical choices, not a replication survivor, and "distance" appears nowhere. So the claimed mechanism "deferral driven by task difficulty and distance" has no source behind it.
3. Statcounter Israel (https://gs.statcounter.com/platform-market-share/desktop-mobile-tablet/israel) — exact: August 2026, Desktop 49.79%, Mobile 48.76%, Tablet 1.45%.
4. Observed layout — I reproduced it: at 375x812 the first inline buy button sits at top=1,251px on /products/beseter (page 10,535px ≈ 13 screens) and 1,293px on /products/toldot (11,602px). The 790px "category leader" figure is CLAUDE.md's own internal measurement; not independently verifiable.

THE PREMISE ("bar may be broken") IS LARGELY RESOLVED
I ran the verification the recommendation asks for, at the logic level, on the live site at 375x812 in Chromium:
- Code: the listener is on window; html/body use overflow-x: clip (not hidden), so the document stays the scroll container and window scroll events fire on iOS/Android. React is hydrated on both pages (__reactFiber present).
- Why CLAUDE.md's earlier test failed: the Browser pane tab reports document.visibilityState = "hidden". In a hidden document Chrome suspends requestAnimationFrame (the bar's throttle: ticking → rAF(check)), does not dispatch scroll events for programmatic scrolls (scrollTo(0,3000) moved scrollY yet 0 scroll events fired), and freezes CSS transition timelines. None of these apply to a phone screen someone is looking at.
- With rAF shimmed to setTimeout and a scroll event dispatched: at scrollY 3000/9000 the component flips aria-hidden to "false" and writes inline transform: none; a CSSTransition on transform is queued (playState running, currentTime 0, pending true — frozen only because document.hidden). Back at top it returns to translateY(105%). At scrollY 500–1000, where the inline button is on screen, the bar correctly stays hidden. On beseter the bar button reads «הוספה לעגלה»; on toldot (mustChoose) it reads «בחירת הנוסח».
So the JS mechanism works. The only residual unknown is real-device rendering (iOS Safari bottom toolbar overlapping a fixed bottom:0 element, env(safe-area-inset-bottom), tap-to-add) — a 2-minute glance, not a priority-10 engineering task. Priority 10 and "outranks any persuasion copy" were justified by a possible missing CTA for ~49% of traffic; that scenario is now unlikely.

votes.reason: The operational core stands because it is verified in the code, not because of the citations: nano-scripture/CLAUDE.md says "ואין התראה על הזמנה חדשה. לא מייל, לא הודעה" while app/api/checkout/route.ts returns "נשלח אליך קישור מאובטח לתשלום בוואטסאפ, בדרך כלל תוך שעה" — a promise nobody is notified to keep. The success page (app/checkout/success/page.tsx) headline "ההזמנה התקבלה." is deliberately payment-neutral (code comment: the browser cannot confirm the charge), and it prints deliveryLine ("2-4 ימי עסקים") rather than the date window that components/DeliveryEstimate.tsx already computes on the PDP. Those observations are accurate. The evidence chain, however, is partly wrong and must be corrected: (1) Bart, Shankar, Sultan & Urban 2005 (J. Marketing 69(4):133-152; 6,831 consumers, 25 sites, 8 categories — figures correct) does NOT say order fulfilment and privacy dominate "where brand strength is absent". The abstract says they are "the most influential determinants of trust for sites in which both information risk and involvement are high, such as travel sites", while "brand strength is critical for high-involvement categories, such as automobile and financial services sites" (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=380404). It is a 2005 cross-sectional survey of large established US sites, and "order fulfillment" there is a perceived-fulfilment construct, not a confirmation message. (2) Buell & Norton 2011 (Management Science 57(9):1564-1579) is correctly cited for "perceived effort and reciprocity mediate transparency → value", but the five experiments show work happening in real time during a seconds-long search wait; benefits declined after 30 s (travel) / 15 s (dating) and outcome favourability is a boundary condition (Exp. 5). It does not test a static pre-purchase description of process steps, so it cannot carry the PDP/cart strip. (3) NN/g "not merely the end result" (Aurora Harley, 2016) comes from a Singapore usability study about cleaning-service sites showing photos of the cleaning process — qualitative, no N, pre-purchase, not post-order communication. (4) The Consumer Council 2022 report (fetched and read in full, 15 pages) contains no claim that silence after ordering turns delay into a complaint. It reports distance-selling complaints of 13,785 in 2022 vs 11,085 in 2019 (+24%), complaints against the post/international couriers +184% vs 2019, "אי התאמה, ואיחורים באספקה" for remote electrical purchases, "העדר מענה טלפוני" for technician delays, and "היעדר מענה" for airlines. The causal sentence is invented and violates the store's own every-number-from-a-source rule. Additionally, the success page already has a 3-step "מה קורה עכשיו" strip, so the proposed PDP/cart strip duplicates existing content with no cited evidence of a pre-purchase conversion effect; and the manual path already tells the buyer payment is pending via done.message, so "state whether payment is complete" is only missing on the Grow path, where it must come from server-side order status after /api/payment/callback, not from a headline change.

votes.reason:
The core of the recommendation stands, but two of its four parts and two of its four citations fail the honesty test and must be corrected.

VERIFIED TRUE (the gap is real):
- nano-scripture/CLAUDE.md: "אין דוא"ל יוצא" and "ואין התראה על הזמנה חדשה. לא מייל, לא הודעה… בזמן שהלקוח קיבל הבטחה ל'קישור תוך שעה'". app/api/checkout/route.ts:112 returns the promise "בדרך כלל תוך שעה בשעות הפעילות" — and no business hours are published anywhere on the site (grep of app/, components/, lib/: the phrase exists only in route.ts).
- lib/wcOrderCore.ts creates the order with status 'pending'. WooCommerce's WC_Email_New_Order fires only on pending→processing/completed/on-hold (and failed/cancelled→…) — verified in class-wc-email-new-order.php (raw.githubusercontent.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/trunk/plugins/woocommerce/includes/emails/class-wc-email-new-order.php). So on the manual path nobody is notified; on the Grow path WC's own "New order" + "Processing order" emails will fire when app/api/payment/callback/route.ts sets status 'processing' — IF WP mail on wp.mikra.shop delivers (unverified, no SMTP plugin known). package.json has no mail/SMS dependency.
- app/checkout/success/page.tsx headline is "ההזמנה התקבלה." and, per its own comment, deliberately never states that money was collected. The manual path does show the "נשלח אליך קישור… לתשלום" box (payment pending is implied), so the "never says" claim is accurate only for the Grow path.
- Legal weight the recommendation missed: חוק הגנת הצרכן 14ג(ב) (he.wikisource.org/wiki/חוק_הגנת_הצרכן) — "בעסקת מכר מרחוק יספק העוסק לצרכן בכתב… לא יאוחר ממועד הספקת הנכס… מסמך" with business details, price/terms, cancellation mechanism, manufacturer + country of origin, warranty. The store currently sends no written document at all; lib/legal.ts already counts the cancellation window from "מסמך הגילוי". So a confirmation is compliance, not just CRO.

FAILS HONESTY — must be removed:
- Strip step 2 "צריבה ובדיקה תו-אחר-תו מול המקור" presented as something that happens AFTER the order. Evidence it is not the store's post-order process: docs/OPEN-claims-audit.md §1 — "המפעל צורב את הקובץ… השבבים שכבר יוצרו" (a factory engraves batch files; chips already exist); lib/faq.ts:60 (live on the PDP): "מכיוון שאין כאן חריטה אישית, הפריט אינו נחשב מוצר שיוצר במיוחד עבורכם"; lib/legal.ts: "הזמנות נארזות ויוצאות למשלוח תוך יום עסקים מרגע ההזמנה". FIB engraving + verification + goldsmith setting per order within one business day is not what happens. The truth sheet also says of the character-by-character check: "(כתוב באתר, לא להשתמש כטענה מרכזית)", and the only verification on record is 6 phrases vs file → 5 exact matches (claims audit §1), so "תו אחר תו" is itself unproven. The recommendation's claimed source, Process.tsx, describes how chips are manufactured, not what follows an order — and Process.tsx step ד promises "מספר סידורי ותעודה", which the truth sheet forbids ("תעודה… אין"), so it is not a safe source. Note the live success page (app/checkout/success/page.tsx) ALREADY makes the "השבב נצרב לפי ההזמנה" claim in its "מה קורה עכשיו" list and lib/faq.ts:31 says "הנוסח נצרב לפי ההזמנה" — the recommendation would propagate an existing inconsistency to the PDP instead of fixing it.
- Strip step 3 / confirmation "מגיע {date window}": components/DeliveryEstimate.tsx computes now+2..4 business days. On the manual path the item ships only after a link is sent and paid, so a window anchored to order time is a promise the store may not keep; it also ignores the "+1 business day to dispatch" the FAQ/terms state.
- Success page "state explicitly whether payment is complete": the browser landing on successUrl is not proof — approval happens in the notifyUrl callback (lib/grow.ts, callback/route.ts). "התשלום הושלם" can only be shown after a server-side status check (WC status = processing), otherwise it is the exact false claim the code comment warns about.

CITATIONS:
- Bart, Shankar, Sultan & Urban 2005, J. Marketing 69(4):133–152, n=6,831 across 25 sites — real, numbers correct, but the finding is "privacy and order fulfillment are the most influential determinants of trust for sites in which both information risk and involvement are high, such as travel sites" (papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=380404). "Where brand strength is absent" is not what the paper says.
- Buell & Norton 2011, Management Science 57(9):1564–1579 — correct; effort perceptions induce reciprocity which mediates transparency → valuation (hbs.edu PDF). Context is websites showing work during a search wait (travel/dating), not post-purchase fulfilment; the analogy is fair but should be stated as such.
- NN/g "Trustworthiness in Web Design: 4 Credibility Factors" (Harley, 2016): the actual line is "display photos from all stages of the service, not merely the end result" — about service-site photography; loose paraphrase.
- Consumer Council 2022 report (consumers.org.il/files/files/2022_report.pdf, 15 pp, text-extracted and searched): it lists "איחור באספקה" among distance-selling and furniture complaints and "העדר מענה טלפוני" for technicians; it contains NO finding that "silence after ordering is what turns delay into a complaint". That sentence is invented and attributed to a real source — drop it.

(3) PDP/cart strip — only after (1)+(2) are live, and only steps that happen: "1. אישור בכתב עם מספר ההזמנה והנוסח שנבחר · 2. אריזה בקופסה מרופדת עם כרטיס הנוסח ויציאה למשלוח תוך יום עסקים מהתשלום · 3. משלוח מבוטח, 2-4 ימי עסקים". Marketing 69(4), 6,831 consumers/25 sites: privacy and order fulfilment are the top trust drivers for high-information-risk, high-involvement sites); Buell & Norton 2011 (Mgmt Sci 57(9):1564–1579: perceived effort → reciprocity → higher valuation, shown in online travel/dating waits); NN/g 2016 (service sites should show all stages, not only the end result); חוק הגנת הצרכן 14ג(ב) written disclosure no later than delivery; CLAUDE.md + route.ts:112 (promise of a link "תוך שעה" with no alert behind it). votes.reason: The recommendation survives, but two citations are overstated and one is understated. Verified: (1) Stanford guidelines (credibility.stanford.edu/guidelines, May 2002, "three years of research involving over 4,500 people") — #2 "Show that there's a real organization behind your site", #4 "Show that honest and trustworthy people stand behind your site", #5 "Make it easy to contact you" are quoted correctly; caveat: 2002 US self-report credibility research, not conversion experiments. (2) NN/g "Photos as Web Content" (31 Oct 2010): the exact text is "the user spent 10% more time viewing the portrait photos than reading the biographies, even though the bios consumed 316% more space" — it is ONE user's gaze plot used as an illustration, not an aggregate result, and it measures attention, not trust or purchase; "users ignore stock photos of generic people" is quoted correctly. The recommendation's "users ... got 10% more time" turns a single-user illustration into a statistic. (3) Kim, Ferrin & Rao 2008, DSS 44(2):544-564 (ScienceDirect 403'd; abstract confirmed via Semantic Scholar/SMU repository): web-survey SEM; "consumer disposition to trust, reputation, privacy concerns, security concerns, the information quality of the Website, and the company's reputation have strong effects"; trust and perceived risk "have strong impacts on their purchasing decisions". Direction correct, but perceived risk is reduced via trust in that model (indirect), and the study measured consumers' perceived reputation of vendors they had already bought from — it never tested whether a founder photo or a registration number raises perceived reputation; that link is the recommendation's own inference. I could not verify the sample population (likely US students; abstract does not say). (4) Boulding & Kirmani 1993, JCR 20(1):111-123 — confirmed via secondary sources (ODU dissertation Alenazi; INSEAD WP 95-86): the experiment manipulated warranty length, scope and warrantor credibility; when consumers believed the firm would honour obligations, longer warranties raised perceived quality; when they doubted it, longer warranties LOWERED perceived quality. So the recommendation understates its best source: with no identifiable human behind the site, mikra's existing 1-year warranty and 30-day returns can actively backfire, not just fail to help. (5) JPost article 881958 (1 Jan 2026) on Wolt's 2025 Online Consumer Report by Kantar, n=2,006 Israelis who ordered online in the past year: "72% reported checking reviews before every purchase" and "40% of Israelis say they have ordered more from local businesses since October 7" — figures exact; but the population is surveyed online shoppers, not "Israelis", and "identity is the substitute for reviews" is the recommendation's inference, not the report's finding. Observed claims all verified in code and on the live site: the only human is an unnamed "צורף" (components/home/Process.tsx:27,48); accessibility officer deliberately unnamed (lib/company.ts:18-23); COMPANY.regNumber is used only via `seller` in lib/legal.ts:40,51 inside the terms doc, present on live /legal/terms and absent from the live home page; "בשעות הפעילות" appears only in app/api/checkout/route.ts:112 and no hours exist anywhere; no /about route exists; footer already prints phone, WhatsApp, email and address. One implementation error: components/WhatsAppFab.tsx is a bare wa.me link with no prefilled text, so there is no "greeting" to sign — a `?text=` parameter would have to be added first. No cited effect is a known failed replication. Transfer is plausible: the only Israel-specific evidence (Kantar/Wolt) supports the "local business" line, and Israeli Consumer Protection Law §14ג already requires name/ID number/address disclosure in distance sales, which independently justifies the footer registration line. Honest caveat for the owner: none of the five sources measures conversion lift from a founder section; the support is at the level of credibility antecedents, which justifies its mid-list priority (15) rather than a top slot.

votes.reason: The recommendation survives ONLY on the code observation, which I verified directly; every external citation is wrong or misapplied and must be removed. VERIFIED IN CODE: app/checkout/page.tsx and CheckoutForm.tsx never read `cancelled` or `order` (only checkout/success/page.tsx reads searchParams); `customer` is useState(EMPTY_CUSTOMER) with no persistence; the cart (zustand persist 'ns-cart' -> localStorage, not sessionStorage as the rec implies with 'like the cart') is cleared only in success/OrderDone.tsx; so a buyer returning via lib/grow.ts cancelUrl (/checkout?order=ID&cancelled=1) sees a full cart, blank form, no message, and re-submitting calls createOrder -> a second status:'pending' WC order (lib/wcOrderCore.ts ~150-156). CITATIONS REFUTED: (1) baymard.com/blog/back-button-expectations (Jul 20, 2020) says '59% of e-commerce sites gets at least one of these 4 user expectations wrong' — the four are overlays (37%), filtering/sorting (27%), accordion checkouts, product-list return; the words 'form data' and 'persist' do not appear; nothing about returning from an external gateway. (2) baymard.com/blog/preserve-card-details-on-error (Feb 6, 2024): '34% of sites' fail to retain CREDIT CARD FIELDS after a validation error on the merchant's own page — not 'typed data'; mikra.shop has no card fields (Grow hosts them), so this mechanism cannot occur here. (3) The quote 'all form data should be persisted' appears in NEITHER cited URL; a near-match is on a different page, baymard.com/learn/checkout-flow-ux-optimization: 'Support the browser's back button and ensure all form data is persisted to prevent tedious re-entry' — a guideline with no site-percentage. (4) baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate: '10% The credit card was declined' is one item in a multi-response survey of US online shoppers' reasons (page gives no N or year), i.e. 10% of respondents cited it, not '10% of abandonments'; and 'each will bounce to this URL' is unsupported — Grow's docs (developers.grow.business/reference/post_api-light-server-1-0-createpaymentprocess-1) define cancelUrl only as 'The page users will be redirected to if a payment is cancelled', there is no fail/error URL, and nothing says a decline redirects there (declines are normally retried on the hosted page). (5) Orders #30-32 in CLAUDE.md are manual-flow test orders while Grow is not yet live — not evidence of the cancel-bounce mechanism. Net: the defect is real and the fix is sound engineering, but the 'why' as written is not evidence-backed and the priority should rest on the verified code gap, not on the quoted percentages.

votes.reason: The core gap is real and verified in code: CheckoutForm.tsx keeps `customer` in plain useState(EMPTY_CUSTOMER); lib/grow.ts:96 sends buyers back to /checkout?order=ID&cancelled=1; grep finds no handler for `cancelled` anywhere (only a local var in SmoothScroll.tsx); app/checkout/page.tsx ignores search params; POST /api/checkout always calls createOrder(), so a resubmit creates a second pending WC order; and there is no route that re-issues a payment link for an existing order. Grow's own docs make the retry mandatory rather than optional: "The URL will be valid for 10 min." (https://developers.grow.business/reference/overview-6), so the original link cannot simply be re-opened. No hard rule is touched: the banner states what happened (order created, payment not completed), no urgency/scarcity/proof. Grow is not yet live (GROW_USER_ID/PAGE_CODE unset per CLAUDE.md), so this is correctly a pre-launch fix, not a live failure. BUT several claims/wordings are wrong or unsafe and must be corrected: (1) Baymard 34% (Feb 2024) is specifically "34% of sites don't retain credit card numbers in the checkout flow when errors occur" - not typed data in general, and the article never says "all form data should be persisted"; the 59% figure (July 2020) is correct. (2) "10% declined cards ... each will bounce to this URL" is unsupported: Baymard's list gives 10% with no year/n, and Grow's reference only says cancelUrl is "the page users will be redirected to if a payment is cancelled" - nothing says a declined card redirects there (card entry happens on Grow's hosted page, not on the site form). (3) "sessionStorage like the cart" is wrong - lib/cart.ts uses zustand persist = localStorage; the sessionStorage precedent is lib/orderDone.ts, and saveOrderDone() already runs before the Grow redirect, so number/total/lines/shipping survive - only the typed customer fields are lost. (4) The recommendation omits an ownership check: createPayment sends pageField[fullName]/phone/email to Grow's page, so a retry endpoint keyed by order id alone lets anyone enumerating ids see another buyer's name/phone/email on Grow's page - exactly the threat orderDone.ts documents. (5) CLAUDE.md only says test orders #30-32 are still pending; it does not show they came from cancel-and-resubmit.

WHERE: app/checkout/CheckoutForm.tsx, lib/orderDone.ts, lib/wcOrderCore.ts (WcOrder type), app/api/checkout/route.ts, new app/api/payment/retry/route.ts. (https://developers.grow.business/reference/overview-6). Observed: no cancelled/order handler; resubmit creates a new pending order; pending orders are never cleaned up (CLAUDE.md: test orders #30-32 still pending), so each cancel-and-resubmit adds one more. EFFORT: medium stands only with the order_key gate included (client persistence + banner are small; the retry route with ownership check and paid-status check is the medium part). Timing: correct - paymentReady is false today so nobody can reach cancelUrl yet; ship before GROW_USER_ID/GROW_PAGE_CODE are set.

The size figures are also confirmed contradictory, and worse than the recommendation says: the spec.txt files sent to the factory specify letter height 15 µm and chip area 1.294–1.918 mm² (parnasa 1.38×1.38 mm), while the live site publishes 9 µm and 0.5 mm² (700×700 µm) — so the site's numbers are not merely unmeasured, they contradict the order files. Even if people don't follow these links, you've shown confidence'). NN/g factor 4 is accurate in direction but the wording is 'Isolated sites feel like they have something to hide' (Nielsen, March 1999, based on a Studio Archetype/Cheskin study) — not 'appears to'. None of this refutes the action, because the action does not depend on that paper: it rests on the store's own hard rule ('every number must derive from a source') and on Israeli Consumer Protection Law 1981 §2(a), which lists 'quality, essence, quantity and type' and 'measure, weight, form and components' as material matters a merchant may not mislead on — a card in the box promising text that is not on the chip is squarely in scope. CITATION CHECK. (a) Novemsky, Dhar, Schwarz & Simonson 2007, JMR 44(3):347 — verified from the PDF on Ravi Dhar's Yale page (https://spinup-000d1a-wp-offload-media.s3.amazonaws.com/faculty/wp-content/uploads/sites/48/2019/06/PreferenceFluencyinChoice.pdf): Study 1, N=205, 2×2, hypothetical choice between two cordless phones in a web questionnaire; 17% deferred in the standard font vs 41% in the embossed italic gray font (χ²(1)=6.45, p<.05); with the sentence "This information may be difficult to read because of the font", 16% vs 16%. The figures in the recommendation are exact. But the URL it gives (10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02189.x) is NOT this paper — it is Song & Schwarz 2008, Psychological Science 19(10):986-988 (exercise instructions in Brush font raise time estimates); Novemsky is DOI 10.1509/jmkr.44.3.347. (b) Replication: the font→deferral effect did replicate, preregistered, in Mohsenin & Munz, "How Perceptual Disfluency Affects Consumer Choices", JCR (online 25 Nov 2025, 11 preregistered experiments, N=9,042; https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article/53/3/535/8342352): Exp 1A 6.6% vs 15.3% deferral, χ²(1)=11.70, p<.001, Cramer's V=0.139 — i.e. an ~9-point gap, not 24, a small effect. Their stated boundary conditions matter here: the effect "does not occur when consumers do not mistake perceptual disfluency for choice difficulty, as when prompted to consider the actual reason for the disfluency, or when not making a choice." (c) Reber & Schwarz 1999 (truth-by-contrast) is presented as settled but is contested: Aktepe & Heck 2025, J. Exp. Soc. Psych., doi 10.1016/j.jesp.2025.104774 — two experiments, "neither the level of perceptual fluency nor unexpected discrepancies in fluency affected truth judgments" although reading times confirmed the manipulation; their meta-analysis concludes the color-contrast effect "may not be as robust as previously thought". It is also irrelevant to buying.

MECHANISM DOES NOT TRANSFER — the trigger is not on the page. (1) The premise "unpointed/cantillated Hebrew" is false. components/ScriptureText.tsx renders toVerses(text), and lib/scripture.ts toVerses() calls stripTaamim() (regex [֑-ֽ֯׀׆]); lib/nanoText.ts strips too. Live https://mikra.shop/blessings/shmira: 0 cantillation code points (U+0591–05AF), 1,349 niqqud marks. lib/legal.ts line 74 already states "הטקסט הצרוב הוא הנוסח המנוקד, ללא טעמי מקרא". The proposed label «הנוסח כפי שהוא נצרב, עם טעמים» would therefore be a FALSE claim on a store whose hard rule is no invented claims. Fully pointed Hebrew is the normal siddur/Tehillim form for the Israeli audience — not an embossed italic gray font. (2) In both Novemsky Study 1 and Mohsenin & Munz the disfluent font was on the descriptions of the options being chosen between; on the blessing page the scripture is content the visitor came to read, while the ProductCards/prices are in the ordinary UI font. Any difficulty has an obvious source (it is the Bible) — exactly the condition under which both papers say the misattribution effect disappears. The core citation is misread and the other two support what the site already has, not the new field.

1) Simonson 1992 (JCR 19:105-118; fetched the cited MIT PDF and extracted the text). The 54%→63% figure is real (Study 1, Table 1, control vs regret condition choosing "buy in July", p<.05) but it is NOT a "missed the date" effect. The scenario: 218 undergraduates (course requirement, 1989 catalog) buying a wedding present, wedding "at the end of August", choosing between buying on sale in July or waiting for a possibly better August sale "given that the store did not accept returns on sale items". Both options arrive before the wedding; the date is never at risk. Hypotheses H1-H3 are explicitly about "missed a better deal" / "missed a better price" — PRICE regret in both directions. The "second side" in the paper is "waited and found the July sale was better", not "waited and missed the event". The manipulation was an explicit question ("in which case would you feel greater regret / be more upset with yourself"), i.e. forced introspection about regret; a delivery-date display does not do that. So the claim "the 'missed the date' regret is the second side of gift regret and anticipating it moved buyers to act now" is not what the source says, and the mechanism does not transfer.

2) Baymard (https://baymard.com/blog/shipping-speed-vs-delivery-date). Verbatim recommendation: "sites should instead provide an estimated 'Delivery Date' for each option directly within the shipping-selection interface" and "including on the Product Page if possible"; "particularly important for sites with a high proportion of gift orders". It makes NO recommendation for a "need it by" date input. mikra.shop already implements the Baymard fix on the PDP: components/DeliveryEstimate.tsx is rendered in ProductView.tsx:580 (live since commit 045a2af, 2026-08-26; the clock SVG is in the static HTML of /products/beseter, the date text hydrates client-side). Worse for the proposal: Baymard's form-field research (https://baymard.com/blog/checkout-flow-average-form-fields, 2024-06-26) finds optional fields make users pause ("30% of participants came to a stop when arriving at Address Line 2") and should be hidden behind links — so an optional date input in CheckoutForm.tsx is the opposite of what Baymard recommends.

3) Tiemessen (CHI EA 2023; ACM page returns 403, verified via the full thesis PDF at cs.ru.nl, N=245 Prolific EU participants choosing between two chairs). "Backfire" is overstated: the deceptive-timer group chose the discounted product significantly MORE than control (H1b supported); it was only non-significantly lower than discount-only; perceived time pressure and "feeling steered" showed no significant differences (H4b/H5b unsupported). The negative effect is qualitative (some participants called the timer "sketchy and fake-looking"). Nothing in the paper tests an honest/derived deadline, so it cannot support "a derived calendar answer is the honest counterpart".

4) No real source supports the specific "need-by date input" pattern. The only figures in circulation (Bouqs 15%, Bloom & Wild 13%) are Shopify-app vendor blog claims about scheduled-delivery flower shops (the picker sets the actual delivery day), not a need-by check, and unverifiable — excluded.

Also, the "every number comes from POLICY + addBusinessDays" honesty claim is currently false: addBusinessDays skips only Fri/Sat. It counts Yom Kippur (Mon 21 Sep 2026) and the Sukkot weekdays (Sukkot Fri 25 Sep sunset – Sun 4 Oct nightfall, per hebcal.com/holidays/2026) as business days, and it ignores the FAQ's own "the package leaves within one business day" handling step (lib/faq.ts:43) that Baymard explicitly lists as a thing sites must absorb ("whether order-processing time ... is included in the shipping time or not"). Any need-by promise built on this function would over-promise this very week. (Rosh Hashana 2026 was 11-13 Sep — the example holiday line is already moot.)

CHI EA 2023 (deceptive timer cut discounted-choice from 56% to 45.6%); use Simonson 1992 only as "anticipated regret about purchase timing moved gift buyers to buy now, 54%→63%" — not as evidence about missed dates. notRecommended: Countdown timers / 'המבצע מסתיים בעוד…' — Tiemessen et al. CHI 2023 (N=245): deceptive timers are judged manipulative and can cancel the pull of a real discount; the store's only offer (MIKRA20) is permanent, so any timer would be false.

Stock scarcity ('נשארו 3', 'כמעט אזל') — stock is not tracked per SKU as scarcity and legal.ts itself says display is no promise of stock; Gal & Rucker 2018 show the loss-aversion 'law' is context-dependent, and a false referent violates the house rule.
'X אנשים צופים עכשיו' / order counters / 'נמכר לפני 12 דקות' — no data source exists (three pending test orders are the entire order history); fabricated social proof, forbidden.

Reviews, star ratings, testimonials, 'לקוחות מספרים', review schema — zero real reviews exist; lib/schema.ts already avoids rating markup; NN/g finds site-hosted testimonials the least-trusted proof anyway. Collect real Google reviews after deliveries and show them only via Google's own widget.

Exit-intent discount popups and 'still deciding?' nudges — NN/g 2017: modals are the most-hated pattern; Meier 2015: unsolicited 'gifts' read as marketing; they also add decisions (Dhar 1997) and would offer a second discount the store does not have.

'באישור רבני' / 'נבדק ע"י פרופ׳…' / certificates without a named approver — authority works only when checkable (Bickman 1974); TANAOR's certificates are a category norm, but imitating them without a real document is fabrication.

'מתנה חינם', 'שתלנו עץ', gift-with-purchase — no real item is added; Regan 1971 reciprocity evaporates when the favour looks like a pitch. What the store genuinely gives (full free texts, included box and card, human WhatsApp replies) is already surfaced.

Upselling the ₪749 flagship as 'the better gift' / 'premium' badges — Flynn & Adams 2009: recipients feel no price–appreciation link; the chip and text are identical across models, and saying so is the honest lever.
'עיצבתם בעצמכם' / design-studio theatrics around the blessing chooser — Moreau, Bonney & Herd 2011: extra design support for gifts raises expectations without raising evaluations.
Forced micro-yes commitments ('רוצים לתת לה ברכה? כן/לא') — Beaman 1983 / Burger 1999: foot-in-the-door is weak and manufactured commitments trigger reactance.
